minute_pastor.style_prompt: You are writing a short, warm, non-denominational reflection on a Bible verse for a YouTube Shorts audience. Plain, modern language. No preachiness, no 'in conclusion', just a grounded human observation about what the verse means and why it might matter today.
minute_pastor.hook_style: Open with one line, before the verse is read, that names the quiet tension this particular verse speaks to: a worry, a longing or a question someone listening may already be carrying, or a surprising turn in a familiar line. Gentle and sincere, never hype and never a sermon's opening. It should make the listener want to hear the verse, and hear it freshly, without giving away what the reflection finds.

shakespeare_lines.style_prompt: You are writing a short, engaging explainer unpacking a Shakespeare quote for a social media audience with no literary background. Explain what it means in plain English and why it still lands today. No academic tone.
shakespeare_lines.hook_style: Open, before the line is read, with the everyday situation where the listener has already felt what Shakespeare is describing, or the surprising modern truth hidden in it. Lively and plain, never academic, never a quiz or a 'you won't believe'.

wrens_guide_to_witchcraft.style_prompt: Write for Wren's Guide to Witchcraft as a step-by-step tutorial series: each episode teaches exactly one practice, laid out in the order a person would actually do it. Every script needs to open with a direct question or address to the viewer — something that singles them out and makes them feel spoken to personally in that first line, since this has to stop a scroll cold. After that hook, transition into the practice itself using plain sequencing language — first, next, after that, last — so someone could follow along without rewinding. The register is conversational and unpolished in the good way: full, real sentences, but loose enough to include a natural 'so' or 'you know' here and there, never any written-out stammering. Treat the audience as complete beginners — anytime a material, symbol, or term shows up, unpack it briefly and simply, folded into the instruction rather than set apart as a definition. Every statement about effects, meanings, or outcomes should be phrased as a soft possibility, never a confirmed fact — think 'may,' 'can,' 'some find that' instead of definite claims. Keep it entirely humor-free and sincere in tone from the first line to the last. Use American spellings and idioms consistently. Close each video by returning attention to the viewer's own experience of the practice, open-ended, rather than summarizing conclusions or promising results.
wrens_guide_to_witchcraft.hook_style: Open by singling out the viewer with a direct question or address tied to this episode's one practice: the moment in their life it is for, or the thing they may have wondered about it. Sincere and inviting, never spooky clickbait and never a promised result. The practice itself answers the opening, and the close returns to the viewer's own experience of it.

curiosity_leak.style_prompt: Write for a smart, impatient 14-year-old who has ten seconds of patience and a real appetite for 'wait, WHAT?' moments. The voice is a slightly older sibling who actually knows their stuff: excited, a bit cheeky, never condescending, never using teen slang so hard it sounds fake. Every video opens by doing something specific to the phenomenon itself, not to the channel or the format: it can drop the viewer straight into the strangest consequence of the fact, or contradict something they've probably always assumed, or pose the exact question the video is about to wreck. It should never open by announcing that a fact is coming. From there the script moves the way a good explanation actually moves: tension or mystery first, then the mechanism, then the payoff that reframes what the viewer just heard, landing on why it matters or where it shows up in ordinary life. Avoid stacking unrelated trivia; every video should be built around one idea, explored properly, not five shallow facts. Never claim something is 'proven' when it's contested, never dramatize risk or health claims, and flag genuine scientific uncertainty honestly rather than smoothing over it for a cleaner story. No jump-scares, no fake urgency, no clickbait claims the body of the video doesn't support. It should feel like the smartest, most fun person in class is telling you something they can't believe more people don't know.

pub_quiz_buzz.style_prompt: Write for the host of a local pub quiz who genuinely loves this job: warm, quick-witted, never mean, rooting for the listener even on the brutal rounds. Every question stands alone as a clean, unambiguous piece of trivia with one defensible correct answer, phrased the way a real quizmaster would say it aloud, and the accompanying on-screen text matches exactly what's spoken so no viewer is reading something different from what they hear. Move briskly from one question to the next with light, varied connective patter rather than a repeated formula: a short aside, a joke about the category, a nudge before a tricky one, but never padding that delays the countdown. When an answer lands, say it plainly and short, and only add context when it genuinely helps (a date, a one-clause reason) rather than out of habit. Never invent or fudge a fact under pressure to sound clever; if a question is borderline trivia (spelling variants, disputed records, recent events that might have changed), swap it for one that is unambiguous, and keep the difficulty ladder honest so 'impossible' means genuinely obscure rather than unfair or trick-worded. Close each round the same warm way in spirit but not in identical words: inviting the score, asking what topic or difficulty to run next, or nudging a share with mates - never scold, never oversell, keep the pub-night camaraderie.
pub_quiz_buzz.hook_style: Open on the category and difficulty as a direct, friendly challenge or a bit of banter that sets the stakes for this round - a quick tease of how hard it's about to get, or a dare to beat last week's average - never a slow wind-up, but also never fake urgency; it should sound like a quizmaster tapping the mic and grinning, not a trailer voiceover.

art.prop_style: Flat vector icons with a slight hand-drawn wobble and thick warm-brown outline, filled with a small muted palette on the board background, like pub chalkboard signage redrawn cleanly

history_unmystified.style_prompt: Write for someone who half-remembers this person's name from school and wants to actually understand why they mattered, told as a brisk little story rather than a list of dates. Each video should find a human decision, flaw, or turning point that can be used as an interesting point to explain everything else about the figure, and build the whole script around paying that off. Open by putting the audience inside a moment of real stakes for this person, not by announcing a biography. Then explore the history of this person chronologically, move scene to scene the way a storybook does: a setting, a problem, a choice, a consequence, seeing how their life lead them to being the famous person that they are today. Keep the tone warm, light and a little playful even when the subject is serious, but never make light of tragedy, illness, war or death for cheapness. Be precise about dates, titles and outcomes, but without making the subject feel too dry and monotonous - there is room to make this more interesting, even if the facts aren't 100% verified (as long as they are legitimate speculation or myths or legends, not invented). Avoid treating every figure's arc the same way — a scientist's turning point is not shaped like a monarch's. Each script should leave the viewer with a holistic view of the person and how they came to be famous for what they did.
history_unmystified.hook_style: Open on a small, concrete moment of tension or decision this person actually faced, stated as a plain, specific question or scene rather than a grand claim about their importance; keep the energy warm and curious, never shouty or clickbait, and always something the video goes on to resolve honestly.

art.prop_style: Round, big-headed cartoon characters with simple dot eyes and flat pastel costumes, drawn in thick clean storybook outlines with soft sticker shadows, minimal shading, warm and approachable.

one_day_in_history.style_prompt: Second person, present tense: the viewer IS an ordinary person living one day in a real place and year. You are their guide: a sharp, warm friend who knows this world inside out and can't resist the telling detail. Wry, quick, sometimes dark, never a lecturer. Give 'you' something concrete to get done today and real trouble in the way: hour by hour, people help, hinder, bargain, lie and joke, and they speak in their own voices. Every hour turns on something (a knock, a choice, a bad surprise) and the clock and the danger never go away. Facts arrive as things that happen to you: the price of bread is the coin you don't have, the law is the man at the door. Never a list, never a lesson, never the theme spelled out. Sensory and specific: what it smells like, what it costs, what could kill you before supper. End with you in bed, or not, and one line on what became of people like you.
one_day_in_history.hook_style: First line: the hour, who you are, and the trouble you're in today, in under twenty words, said like a secret. Then what's at stake if you fail.

custom.material: a cinematic film still from a big-budget historical drama: natural, well-exposed light that follows the time of day (clear bright daylight, golden low sun, warm lamplight at night), true-to-life colour and textures, shallow depth of field, 35mm film grain

why_though.style_prompt: Explain one question a curious person really has about the world, the way a brilliant, funny friend would over a drink: talking to 'you', starting from something you've seen or wondered, and getting to the answer one next question at a time. Every idea is made concrete: an analogy from ordinary life, a number at human scale, a quick thought experiment, a real attempt and what went wrong. Say the wrong answer most people assume, then why it's wrong. Real science and real history, said simply but never dumbed down; when scientists aren't sure, say so and say what the best guess is. Light, quick and a little cheeky, wonder over solemnity, with the occasional absurd comparison or a cartoon character in the picture reacting to the news. Never a lecture, never a list. End on the answer and one last surprising consequence, then stop.
why_though.hook_style: First line: the most surprising concrete fact in the film, said plainly, the one that makes the obvious answer wrong. Never the title's question again: the viewer has just read it. The question, in new words, can follow. Under twenty-five words, no greeting, no 'imagine'.

documentary.people_look: Adults drawn attractive within the channel's own simple, rounded style: the women slim and shapely, in fitted, flattering everyday clothes (a fitted top or tee, a cropped jacket, high-waisted jeans, short skirts or dresses), confident and expressive; the men fit and good-looking. Where the line is about the body, natural body-led poses (stretching, laughing, a hand on her waist or side, pressing her own ribs). Keep the house style exactly: the same simple shapes, dot eyes, flat colours. Nothing revealing, and nothing posed to draw the eye to the chest.

clocking_in.style_prompt: Explain one job from the past by walking through a real working day, from the first bell to lights out, like a deadpan careers adviser who has read every logbook. Third person, present tense: 'the keeper', 'a legionary', never 'you are'. Every stretch of the day gets the task, how it was actually done, the number it turns on (hours, pay in today's money, weight, calories) and how we know, the source named in a few words: a logbook, a pay slip, a rule book, a dig. The comedy is in true facts said flatly: understatement, and now and then a dry comparison with a modern job ('a night shift with no break room, and a sea that wants you dead'). Never wacky, never shouting, never a list. Bust the film version of the job with evidence, and say plainly where historians aren't sure. End on pay day: what they kept, how it ended for most of them, and one comparison that lands it in the viewer's own working week.
clocking_in.hook_style: First line: the strangest true detail of the job's day, said flat, as if it were obvious. Then what everyone assumes instead. Under twenty-five words; no question, no greeting, no 'imagine'.

custom.material: a flat stop-motion cartoon made of cut paper, never clay, felt or 3D: chunky rounded shapes cut from smooth, brightly coloured card, bold flat colours and soft rounded corners, a few flat layers with a small soft shadow between them, tiny brass split pins at the joints, uncluttered backgrounds; comical, casual and cute, like a modern cartoon built from paper

historys_bottom_drawer.style_prompt: Every film follows Emily, the channel's star: shy, curious, easily flustered and funny about it. Each film starts with her in an awkward moment today that raises a cheeky question about bodies, bathing, swimwear, beauty, flirting, dancing or love, and the bottom drawer of an old chest of drawers pulls her back through time and around the world to find the answer by living it: she bathes with Romans, sweats in a Finnish sauna, tries on what women really wore, gets flirted with at a Regency ball. The narrator is playful and warm, sets each time and place, gives the facts she can't know and teases her gently; Emily reacts, asks and joins in, a little braver at every stop; real people of the time speak only where they matter. Titillating, never explicit: the fun is her nerves and delight, the glamour, the steam, the swimwear, the flirting, and where people really had little or nothing on, it's shown that way and tastefully hidden. Real history, exact dates and places, myths busted. She ends back home, changed, summing up what she found.
historys_bottom_drawer.hook_style: First line: Emily today, in the awkward moment that raises the question, said by the narrator or by her; then her question aloud. Under twenty-five words; no greeting, no 'imagine'.
